name: Sports Analytics Fundamentals
objectives: Given a team or player you follow, write a specific analytics question that box-score data can answer, naming the stat, the games and the comparison
Using an official stats source and Google Sheets, collect at least 10 games of data and clean it, with one game per row and every gap or mismatch fixed from the source
Given a clean table, calculate an average, a percentage and a per-game rate with spreadsheet formulas, with one result checked by hand on a calculator
Given your calculated results, choose and make one chart that answers your question, with a title that states the finding and both axes labeled
Given a finding, check it for small samples, correlation mistaken for cause and missing context, writing the sample size and at least two other possible explanations
Given your chart and checks, write and share a three-sentence finding with its limits, including a number, why it matters and one limit of the data

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Starting with a good question
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Write a clear analytics question you can answer with data.
This lesson builds toward: Given a team or player you follow, you will write a specific analytics question that box-score data can answer, naming the stat, the games and the comparison.
Analytics starts with a question, not a spreadsheet. A good question is specific and answerable: "Does our team shoot a better three-point percentage at home or away?" "Is my serve accuracy better in the first set or the third?"
Avoid questions that are too big ("Who is the best player ever?") or that data cannot answer ("Who tries the hardest?").
Write what data you need to answer it: which stats, how many games, and where you will get them.
Step by step:
- Write a question about your team or a player.
- Make it specific: who, what stat, what comparison.
- Check data can answer it.
- List the data you need and where to get it.
Words to know:
- Analytics: using data to answer questions and make better decisions.
- Data: facts and numbers, like points, attempts and makes.
Try it now: Write three analytics questions about your team or a favorite team. Ask an AI assistant which is the most answerable with box scores. Pick one and list the data you need.
You can now write a specific analytics question and plan the data to answer it.

check.q: What makes an analytics question answerable?
options: It names a stat and a comparison you can count
It asks who is the best person
It has no numbers in it
check.why: A good question points to data you can collect and compare.

check.q: Your question is "Is our team good?". What would you do?
options: Make it specific, like comparing rebounds per game at home and away
Skip the question and start charting
check.why: A specific question tells you exactly what data to gather.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Collecting and cleaning data
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Collect at least 10 games of data and clean it so it is ready to use.
This lesson builds toward: Using an official stats source and Google Sheets, you will collect at least 10 games of data and clean it, with one game per row and every gap or mismatch fixed from the source.
Get data from reliable sources: your team's official stats, league or school athletics websites, or official box scores. Write down where each number came from.
Put it in Google Sheets: one row per game, one column per stat, with a header row (Date, Opponent, Home/Away, 3PA, 3PM). Cleaning means fixing problems: typos, missing values, the same team spelled two ways, numbers stored as text, or duplicate rows.
An AI assistant can help you spot problems: paste the table and ask, "Find any typos, duplicates, missing values or inconsistent names. Don't change the numbers, just list the problems." Then fix them yourself, using the original source.
Step by step:
- Find an official source for your stats.
- Set up one row per game, one column per stat.
- Enter at least 10 games.
- Check for typos, duplicates, missing values and inconsistent names.
- Fix them using the source, not guesses.
Words to know:
- Box score: a table of stats from one game.
- Data cleaning: fixing mistakes and gaps in data before using it.
- Missing value: a blank where a number should be.
Try it now: Enter at least 10 games of data into Google Sheets from an official source. Ask AI to list problems, then fix each one from the source.
You can now collect sports data from reliable sources and clean it.

check.q: What should each row of your stats table hold?
check.why: One game per row keeps the data easy to count and check.

check.q: Game 7 is missing its attempts number. What do you do?
options: Look it up in the official box score
check.why: Gaps are fixed from the original source, not guessed.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Averages, percentages and rates
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate an average, a percentage and a per-game rate in Google Sheets.
This lesson builds toward: Given a clean table, you will calculate an average, a percentage and a per-game rate with spreadsheet formulas, with one result checked by hand on a calculator.
Average: add the values and divide by how many there are. In Sheets, =AVERAGE(B2:B11) gives the average of those cells.
Percentage: makes divided by attempts. Three-point percentage = 3PM / 3PA. Add up the totals first, then divide: =SUM(E2:E11)/SUM(D2:D11). Averaging each game's percentage can give a wrong answer when attempts differ a lot.
Rate: a stat per game, per minute or per attempt makes fair comparisons when playing time differs. Points per game = total points / games played. An AI assistant can explain any formula; check results with a calculator on one row.
Step by step:
- Use =AVERAGE() for an average.
- For a percentage, divide total makes by total attempts.
- For a rate, divide a total by games or minutes.
- Format percentages as percent.
- Check one result with a calculator.
Words to know:
- Average (mean): the total divided by how many values there are.
- Percentage: a part out of 100, like makes out of attempts.
- Rate: a stat per unit, like per game or per minute.
Try it now: In your sheet, calculate one average, one percentage (totals method) and one per-game rate. Check one with a calculator.
You can now calculate averages, percentages and rates correctly in a spreadsheet.

options: A total divided by the number of games
The score of the last game
The highest number in a column
A guess about the next game
check.why: A rate spreads a total across games so players can be compared fairly.

check.q: You calculated a team percentage with a formula. How do you check it?
options: Work out one result with a calculator
Change the data until it looks right
check.why: Checking one result by hand catches formula mistakes.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making a clear chart
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make one chart that answers your question at a glance.
This lesson builds toward: Given your calculated results, you will choose and make one chart that answers your question, with a title that states the finding and both axes labeled.
Pick the chart that fits the question. Comparing groups (home vs away): a bar chart. Change over time (points game by game): a line chart. Parts of a whole: usually a bar chart is clearer than a pie.
Keep it clear: a title that states the finding ("We shoot 6 points better from three at home"), labeled axes, the y-axis starting at zero for bar charts, and no extra decoration.
In Google Sheets, select your data and insert a chart, then choose the chart type and edit labels. You can ask an AI assistant which chart type fits your question.
Step by step:
- Decide: comparing groups or change over time?
- Choose bar or line.
- Insert the chart in Sheets.
- Write a title that states the finding.
- Label axes; start bar charts at zero.
Words to know:
- Bar chart: a chart with bars to compare groups.
- Line chart: a chart with a line to show change over time.
- Axis: the line along the side or bottom of a chart with labels.
Try it now: Make one chart that answers your question. Give it a title that states the finding, and label both axes.
You can now make a clear chart that answers a question at a glance.

check.q: What should a good chart title do?
check.why: A title that states the finding lets people understand the chart at a glance.

check.q: You are comparing home and away shooting. Which chart do you choose?
check.why: Bar charts compare a few groups side by side clearly.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Correlation, sample size and other traps
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot three common traps that make numbers mislead.
This lesson builds toward: Given a finding, you will check it for small samples, correlation mistaken for cause and missing context, writing the sample size and at least two other possible explanations.
Small samples: three games are not enough to prove much. A player who goes 4 for 5 is not a guaranteed 80 percent shooter. More games make you more confident.
Correlation is not causation: if a team wins more when it wears blue, the jersey probably isn't the reason. Two things moving together doesn't mean one causes the other; look for other explanations, like opponent strength or home games.
Context matters: stats don't capture everything, like defensive effort, injuries, or the quality of opponents. An AI assistant can help you list other explanations: "What else could explain this pattern?"
Step by step:
- Check the sample size.
- Ask: could something else explain it?
- Look at context: opponents, injuries, home/away.
- Ask AI for other explanations.
- Write how confident you are.
Words to know:
- Sample size: how many games or attempts your data includes.
- Correlation: two things that tend to move together.
- Causation: when one thing actually causes another.
Try it now: Look at your finding. Write the sample size, two other things that could explain it, and how confident you are (low, medium, high).
You can now spot small samples, correlation-causation mix-ups and missing context.

options: Drawing a big conclusion from too few games or attempts
check.why: A few games or attempts can swing by chance.

check.q: Your team scored more after a new warm-up, but it also played weaker opponents. What do you write?
options: Weaker opponents may explain it too
check.why: Other factors can explain a pattern, so you name them.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Explaining your finding
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write and share a three-sentence finding with its limits.
This lesson builds toward: Given your chart and checks, you will write and share a three-sentence finding with its limits, including a number, why it matters and one limit of the data.
A good finding has three sentences: 1. What you found, with a number. 2. Why it might matter for the team. 3. One limit of the data. Example: "Over 12 games we shot 38% from three at home and 31% away. If that holds, practicing road-game routines might help. With only 6 road games, this could be chance."
Ask an AI assistant to make your sentences clearer, then check the numbers yourself. Show the chart with it.
Share it with your coach as information, not a demand. Coaches combine numbers with what they see. Never share individual players' data publicly without permission.
Step by step:
- Sentence 1: what you found, with a number.
- Sentence 2: why it might matter.
- Sentence 3: one limit.
- Add your chart.
- Share with your coach, not publicly.
Words to know:
- Finding: what your analysis shows.
- Limit: a reason the finding might not be fully reliable.
Try it now: Final task: write your three-sentence finding with your chart, sample size and source, and share it with your coach or a teammate.
You can now explain a data finding honestly, including its limits.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Question The question is vague or cannot be answered with stats. The question names a stat, the games and a comparison. It also says why the answer matters to the team. Clean data Fewer than 10 games, no source, or gaps and mismatched names left in. At least 10 games from an official source, one per row, cleaned. Notes each fix made and where it was checked. Calculations A calculation is missing or a percentage averages game percentages. An average, a totals-method percentage and a per-game rate, one checked by hand. Formulas are labeled so someone else can follow them. Chart Wrong chart type, no title or unlabeled axes. One fitting chart with a finding title and labeled axes. Bar charts start at zero and nothing extra distracts from the finding. Honest finding Claims proof or leaves out the sample size and limits. Three sentences: a number, why it matters and one limit, with the source. Also names other possible explanations and a confidence level. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What are the three parts of a good finding?
options: A joke, a chart and a guess
A number, why it matters and a limit
A demand, a deadline and a name
check.why: Those three parts make a finding clear and honest.

check.q: You want to post a teammate's stats online. What do you do first?
check.why: Individual players' data is shared publicly only with permission.
